title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
content:
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery

Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

title: Patriotism, Trump-Style
content:
Steven Nelson, writing for The New York Post:

President Trump claimed Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could have become a leader in China’s artificial intelligence industry if he hadn’t been reinstated to the US firm — telling CNBC in a phone interview that the 63-year-old has “got a little blood there” despite being born in Taiwan.

“If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’ — He’s got a little [Chinese] blood in him. He’s got a little blood there — ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei?’” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview, during which he called Huang, 63, a “national treasure” despite his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that.”

This was during Trump’s 50-minute phoner on CNBC. As I noted yesterday, on his Truth Social blog, Trump wrote:

On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure.

Think about how perverse Trump’s worldview is that he simultaneously declares that Jensen Huang is a “Great Patriot and National Treasure” and that Huang would be justified in moving to China to help the United States’ geopolitical archrival in the AI arms race “if he was treated badly”.

Free lunches (permalink)

An old joke: "Two economists are walking down the sidewalk and one of them points and says, 'Look, there's a $20 bill, right there on the ground!' The other one is dismissive: 'No, if that was a real $20, someone would have picked it up by now.'"

If that joke leaves you scratching your head, then you've been lucky enough to avoid the neoclassical economist's view of the world as a market whose participants, in aggregate, know everything about what people are buying and selling. In that world if there's a "free lunch" – like a $20 bill on the sidewalk – someone will have already taken it.

Likewise, if there's a seller who's priced their goods at $10 and a buyer who's willing to pay $30, there will be an "arbitrageur" who will be shuttling those $10 goods to those $30 customers and pocketing the difference. Give it enough time and either the seller will raise their price to $30, or the buyer will realize they should only be offering $10.

The market will "clear," with everyone getting everything they need in the most efficient way possible, meaning there's no way to improve anyone's position without making someone else worse off:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency

When markets don't behave like this, neoclassicals hunt for "distortions" that prevent the market from performing this continuous balancing trick. "Distortion" is best understood here as a euphemism for "democratic intervention." If you've ever gotten excited about a commonsense policy solution to a serious economic problem (like public grocery stores as a means of addressing food deserts and greedflation), only to see it shot down by economists who use a lot of jargon to "prove" that it can't possibly work, you've experienced how well "distortion" doomerism keeps us from having nice things.

The economist's allergy to distortions is curiously selective. When a company uses its monopoly power to capture its regulators, or bind its workers to silence, or to erect barriers to entry that keep competitors at bay, somehow that doesn't qualify as a "distortion." Same goes for the situation in which a dominant retailer (Walmart) and a dominant manufacturer (Pepsi) come to a secret agreement to force everyone else to raise prices a ton so that Walmart can raise its prices by a (smaller) ton and still be "the cheapest":

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities

Economists are in love with the idea of the economy as a self-licking ice-cream cone, a beautiful machine that operates all by itself, processing all the information we inject into it by buying and selling and finding the optimal way to produce more of the things we want best at the lowest prices.

But like any love-drunk suitor, economists habitually overlook the market's glaring imperfections. In the self-correcting market, a company with high margins sends up a flare that alerts other, hungrier companies to swarm it, competing to offer the cheapest price. Likewise any company with lots of customers: those crowds of customers should conjure up armies of clever planners and inventors who find more efficient ways to produce the same goods and services and lure those customers away.

This is the crux of market orthodoxy, the idea that competition lowers margins, goading sellers to offer better goods at better prices. Don't take my word for it, here's Adam Smith:

It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages.

If this is true, then the surest sign of a "market distortion" is persistent high margins and persistent high market-share. Any company that dominates its market and charges far more than its costs is a crisp, $20 bill lying right there on the sidewalk for all to see. If no one picks up that $20, then it's a sure bet that there's a "distorter" who is preventing the market from acting on the "information" that there is an opportunity here.

America's business lobby loves distortions, so long as they're the kinds of distortions that let the companies safely entrust their $20 bills to the sidewalk without worrying about having them scooped up by a competitor.

Take Big Tech: this is an industry with such persistently high margins and so many customers that there are multiple firms in the sector that were able to piss away hundreds of billions of dollars by manipulating their stock prices with buybacks and building AI data-centers that can never turn a profit:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs

If the market was "undistorted" then anyone this rich and this stupid would be in serious trouble. Ask a neoclassical to explain Big Tech's prolonged, morbid wealth and they'll insist that this means that we're the stupid ones, because we can't play 11-dimensional chess like Zuckerberg, which is why we can't understand why it was good to piss away $80b on the metaverse.

But we don't have to look very hard to find another, simpler explanation. Big Tech owes its profits to its monopoly power, which allows it to form cartels that collude to rig prices:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue

Big Tech has so much money that it can capture its regulators, securing favorable laws that make it literally illegal to build competing products, so we're all stuck as hostages of the platforms:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/14/sole-and-despotic/#world-turned-upside-down

An "undistorted" market is one where information is presumed to flow freely among market participants. But the business lobby has secured far-reaching legal protection for the nondisclosure and noncompete "agreements" it crams down the throats of its workers, customers and suppliers, making it literally illegal to warn other people about the defects in both its products and its managers' character:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/27/zuckerstreisand-2/#autodisparagement

An "undistorted" market is one in which the state intervenes to enforce contracts. Without that intervention, cheaters can beat trustworthy competitors by making promises they have no intention of keeping. Yet, the business lobby has secured government backing for "binding arbitration" waivers that make it illegal to sue people who cheat you, forcing you to have your case heard by a fake judge who works for the cheater and nearly always rules in their favor (and whose rulings are legally secret, so you can't warn others so they don't get cheated as well):

https://pluralistic.net/2020/04/11/socialized-losses/#justice-restored

"Undistorted" markets are supposed to keep firms lean and energetic, forever on the lookout for new ways to attract the best customers and the best workers with the best deals and the best pay. Decades of lax merger enforcement has produced an economy dominated by fat and lazy cartels who substitute bullying and lock-in for innovation and customer service:

https://www.openmarketsinstitute.org/learn/monopoly-by-the-numbers

The business lobby and their tame economists have invented all kinds of gimmicks to "disprove" your intuition that you're worse off every year thanks to cheaters and their rising profits.

For example, there are plenty of mainstream economists who insist that the wage stagnation that has trapped American workers for decades is a hoax. They point to statistics that show that when you include "transfers," American workers are doing just as well as their foreign counterparts, and in particular, that the American public continues to enjoy healthy levels of "consumption" (buying things).

These are very dodgy stats indeed. Here's how they're calculated: the American consumption figures include the health care received by the American public. That health care includes Medicare payments on behalf of Americans who age out of employer-provided insurance, and Medicaid payments made on behalf of poor Americans. These medical services cost 200-300% more than the same services when provided in other advanced economies (Canada, Germany, the UK, etc).

So when a poor American in Buffalo gets Medicaid dialysis at three times the price of a dialysis session in Toronto, that is counted toward that poor person's consumption levels, as though they had just gone out and spent hundreds of dollars on treats from the Cheesecake Factory and the Apple Store. In reality, they've received an overpriced service (whose costs were absorbed by the public purse). They haven't seen an extra dime to spend on either the necessities of life or a little treat:

https://capitalisnt.com/episodes/can-capitalism-be-popular-FcXPThM6

America spends more on health-care than any other rich nation, and gets less for its money than anyone else. In other words: neoclassical economists use the sky-high monopoly prices set by America's overpriced, underdelivering health care cartel to claim that we've got tons of "real" income, because they factor in the hundreds of billions in public subsidy the feds and the states funnel to these persistently high-margin (and therefore definitively inefficient) businesses.

Get rid of the statistical mirages and a very different America comes into focus: one in which large businesses have fused with a corrupted state that serves as bagman and enforcer for the corporate sector as it rips off workers and consumers.

Remember the decades when tech bros insisted that their "disruption" was all in service to shattering the death grip that legacy industries had on our economy? Uber's early champions insisted that the taxi sector had been "distorted" by overreaching regulation. Once Uber injected "information" about willing riders and willing drivers into the system, the market would clear, pairing drivers and riders in such a way that no one could be made better off without making someone else worse off. Today, Uber uses its lock-in to pay drivers less and less and charge riders more and more – and Uber uses IP law to prevent competitors from making an app that lets drivers automatically shop for better pay and apps that let riders find cheaper rides:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/11/your-risk/#my-reward

Uber's "perfect market" is a government-backed monopoly, reliant on the state to block anyone from reverse-engineering its app or unionizing its workers. That fusion of the corporation and the state funnels billions from drivers and riders to investors.

Amazon's founding principle is best summed up in Jeff Bezos's oft-repeated motto, "Your margin is my opportunity." Today, 51-60% of every sale on Amazon's platform is captured by the platform. AWS, Amazon's cloud service, is no longer its most profitable line of business. Today, Amazon's largest source of profit is the $80b it makes every year from charging for search-placement, extracting bribes from sellers to show you items that cost more than the best match for your query:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/04/cheating-at-fraud/#absentee-rentier

That's a lot of margin – and a lot of opportunity.

Same goes for Apple: the company's most profitable line of business is the 30% app tax it levies on every payment made using an iPhone or iPad. Apple makes $100b/year charging a 30% commission on payments that cost the company less than 1% to process. That's a lot of margin.

Then there's the ad-tech duopoly, Meta/Google. These two companies make so much money in an ad system where they represent both buyers and sellers in marketplaces they operate (where they also buy and sell), that they have hundreds of billions left to blow on AI misadventures:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/19/spying-v-context/#unattributed

In other words, Big Tech's sidewalk is covered in $20 bills, which the US government bans American firms from picking up. But that's America. What about the rest of the world?

Well, for 25 years, the US Trade Representative has made it America's business to see to it that every US trading partner enacted laws that protected America's tech companies from competitors. Thus the UK's pavements are littered with 20 pound notes, and the EU's are covered in 20 euro notes:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

The US Trade Rep used both a carrot and a stick to extract these policy concessions from the rest of the world. The carrot was the promise of tariff-free access to the American consumer (the world's richest, shoppingest, most numerous consumer cohort) – the stick was the threat of tariffs.

Today, the stick is broken and the carrot is gone. The American consumer's wallet has been drained. American homeowners groan under multiple mortgages. American renters give 50% of their paycheck to Wall Street slumlords. The US healthcare system has emptied their bank accounts and student debt came for the rest. When American economists have to use the fact that you're too poor to afford overpriced health-care to "prove" that you're rolling in dough, you know the end is nigh. America's growth industries are "financial services" that let you pay for a burrito in four installments – and gambling. The median American worker has $955 saved for retirement:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/12/always-great/#our-nhs

Then there's tariffs: as November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor and flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play." The tariffs Trump imposed on every country in the world (even the uninhabited penguin islands) destroyed tariffs' deterrent value:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations

America's tech margins are the world's opportunity. It's time to move fast and break (tech's) things. It's time to move fast and break kings. Any economist who truly believes in markets would cheer this on: after all, repealing the "market-distorting" laws the US bound the world to can only increase market efficiency, right? Get rid of trade secrecy, nondisclosure and nondisparagement so that market actors have the information they need to make buy/sell decisions. Get rid of IP laws that block reverse-engineering, scraping and other tactics that facilitate switching to a competitor's service, using your own payment processor, or hijacking and rewriting search results to purge paid placement.

Silicon Valley told us we all have a duty to disrupt sclerotic, top-heavy, lazy industries and treat their margins as our opportunity. When they did it to us, that wasn't progress. If we do it to them, that's not piracy.

It's just business.

title: Virgin Media Hub 5 API
content:
I've seen some of these APIs documented around the web, but never in one place. This is a list of generally useful information you can get out of the VM SuperHub 5 (a rebadged Sagemcom F3896LG) - I haven't tried them on the 5x.

These were all tested using modem mode. They should still be the same for router mode - although you'll need to use 192.168.0.1 rather than the listed IP addresses here. You will need to send a User-Agent string with any request. You may also need to ignore the self-signed certificate.

Some of the outputs are fairly large, so I've truncated them for ease of viewing. I've also lightly redacted any sensitive data like MAC addresses.

title: When happens to entries in the CoreApplication Properties when the source apartment shuts down?
content:
Commenter Luca Bacci observed:

Don’t know why, but last I tried the COM static store (runtime class “Windows.ApplicationModel.Core.CoreApplication”) was accessible from an unpackaged, Win32 application. It also seems to tie entries to the originating apartment lifetime (namely: the apartment from which the property is added). Can you shed some light?

First part first: The COM static store is available to all applications.

This API is supported in Universal Windows Platform apps only, except for the Properties property, which is always available.

Okay, now the second part: What happens to the entries in the CoreApplication Properties when the source apartment shuts down?

Nothing.

Nothing happens to them. They are still there. Here’s a demonstration:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <winrt/Windows.ApplicationModel.Core.h>
#include <winrt/Windows.Foundation.Collections.h>

int main()
{
    winrt::init_apartment(winrt::apartment_type::single_threaded);

    std::thread t([] {
        winrt::init_apartment(winrt::apartment_type::single_threaded);
        winrt::Windows::ApplicationModel::Core::CoreApplication::Properties().
            Insert(L"meow", winrt::box_value(1));
        winrt::uninit_apartment();
        });

    t.join();

    auto value = winrt::unbox_value<int>(
        winrt::Windows::ApplicationModel::Core::CoreApplication::Properties().
        Lookup(L"meow"));
    
    printf("Got the value %d\n", value);
    winrt::uninit_apartment();
    return 0;
}

After initializing COM on the main thread, we create a secondary thread, on which we also initialize COM in single-threaded mode, add a value to the Core­Application.Properties called "meow" with a value of 1, and then uninitialize the apartment.

Back on the main thread, we wait for that to finish, and then go to the Core­Application.Properties and ask for the "meow" value, and hey, there it is!

So the entries in Core­Application.Properties do not expire at the expiration of the apartment that added them. But, they do expire when the last apartment shuts down, because that’s when COM shuts down for the entire process.

Next time, we’ll investigate what Luca observed.

title: Taking a password joke seriously
content:
“I’m sorry but your password must contain 1 char each from: Arabic, Chinese, Thai, Korean, Klingon, Wingdings and an emoji”

This was a message from Finley Creative (@FinleyCreative) to Jeff Atwood (@codinghorror) on March 3, 2016. The original post seems to have gone away.

You could write a script to generate a password according to these rules. How secure would it be?

Multiplying the number of characters from each category gives

153 * 20992 * 57 * 11172 * 38 * 196 * 1409 = 21463556813227081728

possibilities. You could get different numbers depending on how you interpret each of the words in the rules. For example, the calculation above counts Arabic and Thai letters, but Klingon counts 26 letters, 10 digits and 3 punctuation marks.

Allowing the characters to appear in any order multiplies the number of possibilities by 7!  = 5040. This corresponds to 76.5 bits of entropy, about the same as 13 alphanumeric characters (upper and lower case).

You could generate a password as above, then using something like Base 58 encoding to turn into something you could type on a standard keyboard.

What if you wanted to use the seven Unicode characters as a password without converting them to ASCII characters first? This would be asking for trouble due to possible different encodings of the Unicode characters. Besides, sites that insist that your password contain a “symbol” can be quite restrictive in what symbols they allow.

title: Do-it-yourself meta-analysis
content:
Dynomight has looked at the health effects of vitamin D supplementation. The large-scale meta-analyses that have been performed conclude there is no significant effect, even though individual studies relatively consistently point in the direction of an effect. This means our failure to detect a significant effect may be due to low experiment power.

Dynomight suggests a mechanism for that: what if the low power of the existing randomised trials is because they tend to be run in countries that fortify common foods with vitamin D? That would mean, practically speaking, all arms of the trial get the treatment, which certainly would make the experiment weaker.

To investigate, Dynomight pulls out a table with the results only from studies where participants entered with relatively low values of vitamin D in their blood.

title: Responding to objections to recursive self-improvement
content:
I responded to the strongest objections that people had about the RSI essay.

Watch on YouTube; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.

Timestamps

(00:00:00) – “Do you have a real job?”

(00:02:41) – Cindy Wu: Is AI research a verifiable domain?

(00:11:10) – corsaren: The overarching objection

(00:12:20) – corsaren: Are the essay’s examples sloppy intuition pumps?

(00:13:51) – corsaren: Is online learning AI’s Millennium Prize problem?

(00:17:39) – corsaren: Is human evolution evidence for transfer?

(00:22:20) – corsaren: Can scaling RL let AIs ramp quickly in new contexts?

(00:25:31) – Why take Paul Christiano’s predictions seriously?

(00:26:26) – Intuitions for what superintelligence could be like

(00:29:26) – Paul’s 2018 prediction and the Hugging Face incident

(00:32:44) – How would superhuman AIs actually take over?

(00:35:12) – What should we do about AI motivations?

(00:40:54) – Séb Krier: Won’t many different models constrain each other?

(00:44:09) – Henry Zhang: Is METR’s finding just one data point?

(00:49:13) – Agustin Lebron: Is it still recursive if humans are in the loop?

(00:53:07) – Peli: Does AI’s success in math transfer to AI research?

(00:56:20) – Henry Dowling: Will AI research be bottlenecked on compute?

(01:00:21) – Takeaways, and the next couple of years

(01:03:30) – Would we even know?

(01:03:57) – Closing thoughts

Transcript

(00:00:00) – Intro

Dwarkesh Patel 00:00:00

Okay, so I recently released this essay and this video about recursive self-improvement and why I expect superintelligence by 2030. A wild claim, and understandably, lots of people had objections. Many of them are actually quite interesting and compelling, and I want to go through them here. And by the way, I’m joined by Max Farrens, who is my General Manager, and we ended up discussing all of these ideas as we were writing them down. And in fact, we paired in a lot of the writing.

(00:00:24) – Jim: “Do you have a real job?”

Max Farrens 00:00:25

I think a good place to start is with a comment on the Substack version of the post that comes from a user named Jim, who writes as The 1690 Project. “Dwarkesh, do you have a real job where you use this stuff” (meaning AI) “in and day out? I am guessing you do not, because I do, and this is not what I am seeing at all.” What do you think?

Dwarkesh Patel 00:00:47

Those are two different questions. Do I use these things day in, day out? Yes. Do I have a real job? Debatable. Don’t answer that. Funny that the guy’s like bragging about having a real job. He’s like, he’s like a gotcha on me. Like, I’ve been one of the main people who for the last year and a half has been arguing that the basic learning capabilities that these models lack do in fact impair their productivity. I think people who a naive understanding of what it means to automate a job just look at a system like GPT-6 and say, oh, why can’t we have AGI? It can automate all the white-collar work. I think this is totally wrong. The point I’m making in this essay is that are currently worse than humans at almost everything, right? IT is 1% of the economy, well-scoped coding tasks is a small fraction of IT. In some things, AIs are in fact getting to human level or beyond human level, where we have lots of verifiable proxies. And I would argue that just like math, AI research has a lot of verifiable proxies. And so the consequences of narrow progress in AI research or towards AIs that can do AI research leads to general improvements in AI capabilities. So if you look at a system like GPT-3 and you compare it to GPT-6, GPT-6 is also narrow intelligence, right? It can solve Millennium Prize problems, but it can’t be my video editor. So it can do basically everything way better than GPT-3. What I am imagining is that disproportionate progress in ML research, or AIs that are good at doing ML research, will compress as much progress as we had between GPT-3 and GPT-6 into a single year. And so the end result is within a year of having a system like GPT-7 or GPT-8 or whatever it ends up being, we end up with systems that are more generally capable in the way that humans are generally capable, and are on track to then rapidly become better than humans at everything.

(00:02:41) – Cindy Wu: Is AI research a verifiable domain?

Max Farrens 00:02:42

So Cindy Wu writes on X, “Dwarkesh conveniently sweeps under the rug that climbing a metric involves defining it. Supposing you define it in a way that avoids Goodharting, reward hacking, etc., you need data and environments which do the lifting on defining good metrics. This is most of the game of making AGI, converting fuzzy concepts to formalized objects you can climb without gaming, which requires costly fixes later. He elides the hard problem by saying AI will just automate data.”

Dwarkesh Patel 00:03:12

I think there’s two parts to Cindy’s objection here. One is: can we find metrics which capture general AI progress? Are we aware of such metrics? And two, will we be able to generate the data that makes AIs good at getting better at those metrics? A big part of my essay was dedicated to articulating what those verifiable proxies for general AI progress are, right? So in pre-training, the loss on a held-out corpus is not only a proxy for pre-training progress, it is the basis of pre-training progress, and that is extremely verifiable. And there’s a lot of other proxies you can come up with that are just general intelligence capabilities that are kind of agnostic for any given paradigm. For example, how fast do you master a video game you’ve never seen before? This is one of the key ways that humans are different from current AIs, that humans master new video games really rapidly. How fast can an AI that has only seen a data corpus up to 1700 figure out general relativity? How many open math problems can it solve, right? So there’s a lot of paradigm-agnostic, hard metrics of progress we can come up with. The second argument here is learning algorithms. The application of learning algorithms is very general. The transformer was invented to beat the existing state of the art in translation, but because that architecture, or the implications of the architecture, were general, it also was really good at predicting the next token in WikiText. It’s also really good at generating images and so on. And similarly with reasoning models. Initially they were invented and they were debugged to, like, solve high school math problems and simple coding problems, and now they’re applicable and useful across lots of different domains. And so the breakthroughs that are made in AI end up being measurable on lots of different metrics. And the reason they’re measurable across lots of different metrics is because AI, or intelligence, is general, and because of that, its general improvements show up and make contact with reality in lots of different ways.

Max Farrens 00:05:14

So you started out by saying that there were two subpoints you wanted to address. The first is around verifiable proxies, and I think I understand that your answer is something of the sort of: it is not just that there are verifiable proxies that we can hill-climb, they are, like, the things themselves that we can work on. And so AI research makes itself particularly amenable to hill climbing. The second is around how we actually get the data to do that sort of work, and that is the part I don’t think I understand. So I’d be curious what your thoughts are.

Dwarkesh Patel 00:05:44

Max Farrens 00:37:40

Dwarkesh Patel 00:37:41

Of course, if we get a software-only singularity, which is the thing that a lot of people are worried about, where you radically... this sort of recursive self-improvement loop radically takes you to the ultimate limits of AI population sizes, AI speed, AI intelligence, AI capabilities, the institutions that different AI... the agent society institutions, then maybe that is enough. But I think that is another source of consolation. I do agree that there’s a sense in which, if you’re just like, “Oh, we won’t see anything like this until the AI takes over the world,” I do think you have a very unfalsifiable theory of the world. Now they might retort, “Well, you just saw a Hugging Face. Max Farrens 00:40:54

Excited for it.

Yeah.

Yeah. Context, by the way: METR found that Anthropic’s rate of AI progress on well-scoped tasks is currently two times what it was a year ago. in July or something.

I think you’re absolutely right. Max Farrens 00:49:14

Yeah, so there’s this Twitter thread by Agustin Lebron, who I think you’ve actually had on the show in the past.

Dwarkesh Patel 00:49:19

Yep.

Max Farrens 00:49:19

It’s quite thorough. A particular point I want to go into. And I think it’s worth saying ahead of time that he starts this whole thread by saying the essay actually updated him significantly in the direction of short timelines, RSI, etc.

Dwarkesh Patel 00:49:33

You don’t need to make me feel good.

Okay, sorry, get to the point. So basically he says something like this: “Even if I grant that AI use dramatically accelerates progress, that still does not imply recursive improvement. Dwarkesh Patel 00:49:53

I think that’s correct. Max Farrens 00:52:49

So your claim is like, sure, can still see a lot of uplift and a ton of acceleration even if it’s not definitionally fully recursive right now. Dwarkesh Patel 00:52:49

Yes.

Max Farrens 00:53:07

So RSI essay relies a lot on some sort of correspondence between the progress that we’ve seen in math and the progress that we might see in AI research. And so there’s an objection to this comparison that comes from Peli, writing in a newsletter called Humans on AI. And the objection is, “A potentially major factor in AI’s superhuman mathematical productivity is that before AI, quote unquote ‘experiments’ in math were extremely time-consuming and human-resource-constrained. Dwarkesh Patel 00:54:11

Yeah. I mean, I buy that the relative uplift might not be as big. Paul Christiano, who used to be a computational complexity theorist, said that in his field, it feels like the last month of AI progress, or even the single day of math proofs that AI dumped, sorry, OpenAI dumped in October, if that had happened over a decade, it would be an unusually productive decade of mathematics. So there you’re seeing more like a 100x speedup, plausibly even more. And because of this experiment compute issue, I believe it would probably not be as much progress compressed into a short amount of time as we’ve seen in mathematics. That’s why there’d be these diminishing returns I talked about in the main essay and I’m talking about now. And not only that we should expect it to happen among neglected Erdős problems, but in Millennium Prize problems? Maybe some people were saying it, but almost everybody I have talked to, including the people who are most bullish on AI progress, were not expecting that. And agreed, there will be diminishing returns. It won’t be as fast as mathematics. If it’s a tenth as fast, that would still compress a crazy amount of ML progress into a single year, enough to give us superintelligence by the end of that year.

Max Farrens 00:56:21

Fair enough. Dwarkesh Patel 00:57:01

So he’s totally right that keeping the current rate of compute growth going, that exponential rate that labs have to undergo year after year, is necessary just to keep the current rate of progress going with human labor. And my arguments about why AI progress will speed up, despite that, are about why we should expect both the automation of AI research soon and that to speed up AI progress a bunch more. Is right that if that doesn’t happen by 2030, then because this experiment compute growth or a plateau, so we’ll be spending double-digit percentages of GDP on compute by that point, that the 4x-ing can no longer continue. And so progress will slow down. Then there’s a question of, well, how much is AI progress going to be sped up once you automate it? Bottleneck for experiments is severe because without that bottleneck, you would have an overnight singularity. And instead, because of that bottleneck, you’re gonna only be compressing three to six years of progress over one calendar year. Now, my not so crippling that it will totally wipe out the advantages of automation. Just consider the fact that AI systems are faster than humans who are doing the same work. For example, there’s this benchmark called GDPval, and OpenAI found that GPT-5.2 completes tasks on that 10 times faster. There’s not a super clean way to compare human. I mean, if you look at human thinking time, thinking speed or writing speed compared to how fast AIs output tokens, it’s way more than 10x. There’s a fact that the AIs are working around the clock and they’re also working weekends. So there’s another 5x from that. So basically, in the same calendar week, an AI system can get 50 times the amount of work done that a human can get done. Now, what is the consequence of this? Well, it’s not that algorithmic progress will happen 50 times faster because the researchers are 50 times faster. That’s because the compute for experiments is not 50 times faster. However, would you see some speed-up? I would argue yes. And here’s the analogy or the intuition for why. This actually comes from an essay that Eli Lifland and Ryan Greenblatt wrote. And consider a symmetrical version of what this sped-up automated firm will look like by considering what a slowed-down firm would look like. So let’s call this Sloth AI. And then Sloth AI is full of extremely lazy researchers who only do an hour of work a week. They wouldn’t be going 50 times slower because during that whole week their experiments can keep running, but how many carefully designed experiments can they really design within their one hour based on interpreting all these old experiments? It’s very reasonable to assume they would be going at least a couple times slower, maybe like five times slower. The important thing is that compared to the automated firm with AI systems that are each individually able to do 50 times as much work in a calendar week as humans, the human version of OpenAI is Sloth AI, right? This is a totally symmetric scenario. Imagine if every time an AI researcher did an experiment, equivalent of a decade of thinking went into, okay, how exactly do I interpret what we got here? And let’s really think about every single loss spike across this whole run. It would be very implausible if that firm would not be going any faster than the current version of OpenAI.

Max Farrens 01:00:22

Yeah, that makes sense to me. So as I’ve gone through a bunch of these different objections, like, to prep for this conversation, I had a few takeaways. Is incredibly important to make very clear, especially because we’re talking about potentially insane worlds, what you actually think versus, like, what you think is reasonable or possible or plausible. Like, there’s all these sort of muddy concepts. I think by the end of next year, we’ll have systems that you actually can describe as a competent colleague who is 24/7 working for you. I think current personal assistant type things like Muse or Duet or Dot are very weak versions of what we will see over the next year, where does feel like there is somebody on Slack who’s like, you can just, like, hand off assignments, and very open-ended assignments. Max Farrens 01:02:32

Yeah, interesting. Just like AIs can already do a lot of things that humans can do now, but just sort of at, like, a very mediocre, passable level. But it’s like if you want to do it at a really high bar, if you have a high bar, you’re still gonna hire humans. That’s sort of your argument.

Dwarkesh Patel 01:02:44

Like, some parts of software are like this today. And I think that will happen for a wider range of knowledge work tasks. Yeah, I don’t think we’ll see the intelligence explosion next year. I expect that will happen from 2028 to 2029, basically. And so we will see, the publicly deployed systems will continue getting better in this way. The internal systems, because AI companies will be specifically trying to make their systems especially good at RSI, especially good at doing ML research, they will just have, like, the way that software is way ahead of video editing right now, ML research will be way ahead of video editing in the future. And I’m really concerned about that, obviously.

(01:03:30) – Would we even know?

Max Farrens 01:03:31

Do you think if ML research is as far ahead of these other things as software engineering is ahead of other domains right now, we’ll even know? Like, there is more of a push towards keeping the top models unreleased and using them internally. Like, there’s a chance that the intelligence explosion is happening, we’re not even seeing it.

Dwarkesh Patel 01:03:49

I mean, RSI is happening and we are seeing it, I guess. But AI companies are uplifted right now by AI help.

Max Farrens 01:03:56

Yeah.

(01:03:57) – Closing thoughts

Dwarkesh Patel 01:03:57

Now that we’ve gone through a bunch of the objections, and I’m sorry if I’ve neglected any other compelling ones. Maybe stepping back, I’m like, I’m frustrated by the frame that this conversation is under, where no argument about the future you can, like, prove as if it’s, like, a mathematical theorem. You just have to rely on the back-and-forth arguments, the discourse, just want people to, like, take it seriously that it might happen. In fact, when you talk to these skeptics and you say, like, okay, do you think this could happen, though? Like, what, if you consider this rebuttal to your objection, it’s like, I give a 10% chance, or I give you 20% chance that we’ll have superintelligence in three years or four years. And that’s a lot. That’s not even that much lower than my probability. And take seriously what that means. Like, this is a very serious issue. And I just feel like people are kind of disconnected from, well, okay, I’ve brainstormed one plausible objection to one part of the story, therefore everybody who has even thought about this is crazy. And just keep an open mind to these arguments. But also, yeah, it’s very reasonable to be skeptical. I am skeptical of big parts of this. Yeah, that makes sense. Thanks for coming on the Dwarkesh Podcast.

Let’s be clear about something: this is something you do when an industry is extremely brittle and showing signs of collapse. Jensen Huang may be the founder, but his ouster should not be so systemically important that it causes the market to gain what experts call “Budd Dwyer press conference” vibes. It suggests that everybody realizes that this thing is a bit fucked without one insane, horrible and abusive sociopath wielding NVIDIA’s balance sheet like the reserve bank during a great financial crisis, except working in reverse so that the semiconductor industry can scam the software industry and venture capital out of every dolar in their pockets, along with hundreds of billions of dollars of private credit, along with the retirement and insurance funds. 

So much money has left the system and been funnelled into so few hands as a result of Huang’s craven beat-and-raise machine, and when it eventually falls apart, the damage will be horrendous, and many people will have celebrated this event, unaware that it made things worse. It has revealed many people to be on the side of capital in a way that has made people take sides in both encouraging and discouraging ways, and it will be difficult to look back from here.

Those celebrating Jensen’s return are willing to look away from what is a gratuitous, multi-billion dollar chip smuggling operation that flagrantly violates US trade law, along with a man who preyed on his female subordinates. They are celebrating a lawless and amoral tech industry, and the market’s reaction has been a tacit admission that the market has become, as I discussed last week, an NVIDIA bubble sustained through symbolic gestures and dodgy financial engineering. If you need further proof, check out Anthropic’s stock, which dropped 1.43% as other tech stocks pumped by more than 10%.

Jensen Huang Is A Monster

Oh, and per the Wall Street Journal story from earlier, Jensen Huang has been given the title of “UltraPervert,” taking the affair count up to somewhere above four, but potentially even more than that:

Huang disclosed to the board additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported, but he was contrite about his behavior, people with knowledge of the discussion said.

Jensen Huang is a piece of shit and a worthless excuse of a man that has shown a deep disrespect for his wife and family. His contempt for his fellow human being is also clear from the way that he treats his employees, per the New York Times:

He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.

If your spouse or loved one speaks to you in this way, you are the victim of abuse. This is not how people should talk to other people in any scenario. It is not the right way to treat a person, under any circumstance, for any reason, for any return on doing so. It should be seen as disqualifiable on both moral and legal grounds. To normalize it is dangerous to the fabric of society. This is the CEO of the largest company on the stock market, and he is acting like a fucking monster. We must show him constant, unerring revulsion. To do so is our moral imperative. If you think this is acceptable, you are a fucking freak. 

I must also be clear that Jensen Huang would not say this stuff or act in this disgusting way when faced with anyone who was not financially or reputationally dependent on him in some way. He would not go to Fenway Park and tell some random Southie that he would rip off their head and piss in the hole, because they would fold him up like a fucking deck chair. He speaks this way because he knows that these people can’t fight back, because he has made it quite clear he would use his money and power to harm them further. 

The world should exile somebody who acts with such unrepentant anger. Jensen Huang is a coward insulated from reality by his money and greed, and I believe that the cult that worships him — by which I mean the value of NVIDIA stock — is leading the tech industry to ruin. He is an evil man, and the people who defend him are equally evil, endorsing repulsive and morally abhorrent behavior in their obsession with growth.

Jim Cramer Is A Scumbag

Anyway, Investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald, owned by the children of Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick who reportedly slow-rolled export controls that would’ve slowed NVIDIA’s revenue from China, said that “all’s right with the world,” a statement that doesn’t really make sense unless you are lying or stupid. You choose which. I’m not in the mood.

I find the whole situation disgusting, made more so by the reactions it’s elicited from some of the worst people in tech and finance. Jim Cramer is a fucking monster — or another word beginning with a C — that celebrated Jensen’s return by huffing and puffing about his greatness and smuggly saying that nobody went to jail during the great financial crisis and that “this is over…you can do whatever you want,” and I’ve seen multiple reporters celebrating the “huge surge for equities” that followed the President forcing the return of a man that is obviously, blatantly crooked. The little hand gesture that Jim does when he says “whatever” is enraging. This is a despicable human being with a national audience that should’ve been removed from the airways decades ago. He is the enemy of the common man, and a living, breathing propagandist for the worst excesses of capital itself.

Less than two weeks ago, Cramer was castigating Huang for sex with subordinates, saying that “just because someone is brilliant [it] doesn’t mean he can do what he wants.” Cramer and his ilk are amoral psychopaths masquerading as the ensouled. They are evil, and we should not shy away from saying so. 

Every tech executive applauding Huang’s return is complicit, and actively stating that they believe one’s importance at a tech company means that they should be free from consequences. In their eyes, Jensen’s value at NVIDIA supersedes any need for punishment or exile — one can illegally smuggle chips and fuck your coworkers with abaddon if you’re rich and powerful enough, or if your company’s value makes up 5% or more of the S&P 500. 

And as I’ve discussed, Jensen’s “value” at NVIDIA is his “balance sheet as a service” model involving pumping over $100 billion into the AI industry (per the WSJ) across 293 deals since 2023, and that’s before you include backstops and vendor financing schemes that, per the FT, amount to a little under $700 billion. The sheer scale of NVIDIA’s circular financing operation is a con perpetuated by one man — Jensen Huang — that fills in the financial gaps in an industry that would collapse if he didn’t step in and backstop CoreWeave’s leases, sink billions of dollars into failing AI startups like Perplexity, or provide non-specific vendor financing to Oracle, per TD Cowen.

By the way, isn’t it weird that Oracle, a mere minute after market close on Friday, had to state that it not only had all the money it needed to fulfill its OpenAI contract, but that “any media reports that will come out and say the contrary are incorrect and wrong”? Isn’t it also weird that it mentioned “vendor financing” as one of the ways it had “fully funded this investment cycle”? 

We still don’t know what that vendor financing means, how big it is, or even what the terms are. 

But its existence proves that liquidity is the next great issue of the AI bubble.

This Only Prolongs The Inevitable 

The AI industry would cave in on itself without NVIDIA, and nothing about Jensen’s return fixes any of its underlying problems. As reported by the WSJ a few weeks ago, NVIDIA has “an “avalanche” of purchasing commitments [that] threatened the company,” and all reports suggest that its balance sheet is reaching its breaking point with regards to how many tens of billions it can pump into the ecosystem. Jensen Huang’s return did not fix the lack of ROI, or magically install and power the over $200 billion in NVIDIA GPUs currently sitting in warehouses, or fix CoreWeave’s debt problems, or really do anything other than prolong the inevitable.

Anthropic’s $895 billion in commitments did not disappear overnight, and its IPO has been anything but successful, its brief pop to about 30% over its listing price of $83 met with a slow, painful decline to around $86 to $87 a share, leaving it with a market cap of around $1.17 trillion, with its free-floating shares to nearly double from a little over 1.4 billion shares as of today to over 3.3 billion as of its Fiscal Year 2026 earnings sometime in February or March. It also pushed its bank Morgan Stanley to exercise its “greenshoe” option before the second day of trading, removing a 147 million share buffer that could’ve been used to buy up the stock at the market if it dropped under $83, all because it wanted another $12.2 billion.

Anthropic’s IPO was, as I said before it happened, exit liquidity for its founders, staff and VCs, rushed out to make it seem that it was a completely different company to the one that investors believed using financial engineering to make it seem “profitable” for a single quarter, all before hundreds of billions of commitments began. Around six months from going public, around 9 billion shares of Anthropic stock can be traded on the market, and based on the activity so far, they’ll be dumped en masse. 

And let’s be clear how bad all of this is for OpenAI. 

When Bloomberg covered it raising $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, it specified that “the funding was wired to the company as of Friday,” a peculiar addition that I’ve never seen in the hundreds of different funding stories I’ve read in the last 18 years, suggesting that OpenAI needed somebody, somewhere to know that it actually had real money. This may be connected to reporting around its Q3 numbers, which revealed it had a $10.9 billion operating loss on $10 billion in revenue, which in turn suggests that $11 billion wouldn’t cover even half of a quarter’s expenses.

OpenAI will need money in the next few months, and it’s unclear, given that its private valuation is clearly bullshit when compared to the “real” one given to Anthropic by the market, how it intends to raise it. A down round? Another suicide round? Another half-hearted attempt at a sovereign wealth fund? All of these ideas — like bringing Jensen back — are an attempt to delay an inevitable liquidity crisis which Altman likely hopes the government will step in to fix. 

While I may have been early, I am not wrong. OpenAI is at the edge of the abyss, along with the rest of the AI industry. Only Anthropic was smart enough to rifle through the pockets of the public markets, knowing that the first one out the door would get the real money, its underwriters would get paid, and the market would immediately say “hey man, you seem to lose billions of dollars, what’s that about?” 

The money is running out — even Elon Musk is saying there’s going to be a funding gap of hundreds of billions of dollars in 2027 — and all this cronyism has done is prolong the collapse. 

Interest rates remain high, and are likely to go up. There’s not enough land or power. AI startups require too much money, are all unprofitable, and make up around 80% of Anthropic and OpenAI’s revenues, meaning that the bottom will eventually fall out from both of them at some indeterminate time. Anthropic’s putrid IPO has made it clear that there won’t be any easy SPAC-esque dumps onto retail investors for anybody else, and there’s just no reason to acquire one of these companies. They’re all basically wrappers for closed or open source models. None of this changed because of Jensen, other than his ability to drain further money from the company’s balance sheet, running the beat-and-raise machine as hard as possible until it finally breaks.

To celebrate Jensen Huang’s return is to celebrate a coward, a crook, and a liar, and to directly state that you believe one’s financial performance — even when it’s inherently crooked, circular and rigged to blow — should render any moral or legal consequences moot. 

This is a moment where you, as a member of the tech industry, are showing everybody who you are, what you think, what you believe in (if you believe in anything), how you believe women should be treated in the workplace, how you believe men should be treated in the workplace, and how much of a willing stooge or accomplice you are for the worst excesses of the Rot Economy’s growth-at-all-costs, No IT Loads Refused party. 

Sidenote: The AI photo of Jensen Huang holding a bra posted by Donald Trump is deeply offensive to Huang’s wife and any woman working at NVIDIA, a tacit admission that the rules do not apply if you are a man with enough money and that women are only accessories to their “greatness.” It’s pathetic. Anyone condoning the reinstatement of Jensen Huang approves this image and anything it implies. 

And I just have to ask, what happens now? How does Jensen pump this stock further? The circular financing has started to freak people out, even NVIDIA’s massive balance sheet can only take so much, and, per Bloomberg, ING received “muted” demand when it tried to sell off $500 million worth of data center loans, suggesting that the market just doesn’t want this shit anymore. 

Huang’s return fails to provide any meaningful answer as to how its beat-and-raise machine will continue or how the AI industry will expand much further, and his affair has created a renewed and intense scrutiny of NVIDIA’s growth. 

The New Palace of Versailles Is On Fire

I’ve heard from a lot of people today that feel scared that this somehow restores the entire AI trade or fixes every problem — a simplistic and childish solution to many complex problems.

All it’s done is prove that Trump is desperate to stop the stock market from cratering further, pissing off even hardline GOP allies like Tom Cotton, though I’ll believe they actually give a shit when they do something. It is an unprecedented act of kleptocracy and grift made mere months before the Democrats control both the Senate and the House, at a time when regular people are furious that everything — including the consumer electronics made more expensive by NVIDIA’s sales of warehoused GPUs — is more expensive, and that the rules don’t seem to apply if you’re wealthy. 

Trump has given Democrats an unbelievably easy way to crucify him. It is objectively true to state that he intervened to restore an executive that cheated on his wife three times, once with an alleged Chinese spy, and assisted in over $11 billion worth of sanctioned semiconductors being sold through her company to China. Whether or not you believe that it’s dangerous for the Chinese to have these chips, there are very clear laws, they were violated, and it’s apparently fine as long as you’re wealthy and holding up the stock market.

And this has revealed how many utter cowards loiter in the highest rungs of the tech industry, none greater than Sam Altman, who tweeted “Jensen!” because he is too much of a fucking loser to actually say that he supports him, knowing that Democrats are staring at him. 

This industry is run by greedy little wimps that believe in nothing other than growth, and they’re absolutely fucking terrified. Their garish whining about bringing Jensen back was their admission that the AI industry is specious. It does not have the cashflows to sustain itself without continual subsidies from venture capital and NVIDIA, its largest companies in functional default, its most famous executives known more for their offensive personalities than anything about technology. 

They feel the hand of the reaper on their shoulder, and are fully aware that the money is running out. Nothing has changed. Nobody is more solvent. Token spend has plateaued for months, and token prices are collapsing as AI labs cut prices to compete with both their closed and open source competitors. NVIDIA does not magically have more demand for its GPUs. In fact, it has less thanks to the Huang affair leading to the closure of a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent NVIDIA GPUs remotely from countries like Malaysia, which has already led to the cancelation of a $150 million order from Chinese AI lab Moonshot and halved the value of Southeast Asian neocloud Aaolani, with Jefferies estimating that these rules could kill $44bn to $62bn of NVIDIA”s FY2028 revenue. 

Put another way: Jensen Huang’s return doesn’t change that his customers are increasingly struggling to pay for his GPUs, and their customers are finding it increasingly difficult to afford to rent them.

They are going to run this thing into the ground, and do everything they can to pretend that we’re “back on track,” whatever that means. This situation will embolden them to take more risk, burn more money, ignore more warnings, be more brazen, and burn themselves out far faster and harder than you’d ever imagine. And when you listen to them talk, they speak from a place of fear and with the mindset of peasants, desperate to kiss up to whatever authority figure they see as most dominant at any given time, the conga line of pathetic courtiers and scheming viziers like Brad Gertsner and Gavin Baker making Silicon Valley feel a lot like the 1700s era Palace of Versailles.

Do not be afraid of those celebrating this event as some “return to normal,” because nothing has changed other than the symbolic return of a disgusting oaf at the behest of some of the weakest men ever born. 

The AI industry has always used quasi-religious symbology and deception to make you think that it’s stronger than it is, so I’ll speak plainly: this industry is, for the most part, functionally in default, the money is running out for both data centers and AI startups alike, and the tumbling value of AI stocks was giving — and will eventually continue to give — everybody too obvious a signal that things were (or are) collapsing. 

It all comes down to when the money runs out, and the pervert bounce doesn’t change a thing.

title: Blogger broke the lightbox
content: Some regular readers have alerted me to the fact that the Blogger lightbox for images isn't working. This is a photo-heavy blog, so that's a problem. Although I use a lightly modified basic theme, I did a test post with a current theme and it still didn't work, on Edge, Firefox, Safari and Chrome, so I don't think it's something I did. The offender appears to be, in the minified JS, a couple instances of things like <tt>var Zp={}.getUniqueId("photofactoryservice");</tt> which is of course nonsense because you can't get <s>blood</s> a function from a <s>turnip</s> empty object and I don't see an obvious proto that would provide it. I also looked at a few other blogs and they seem to be similarly affected, so I think this is global and the whole thing feels like a flubbed deploy that didn't get enough testing. In the meantime, you can right click on an image and open it in a new tab to see the larger version, or you can use the mobile view (append <tt>?m=1</tt> to the URL) which doesn't use the lightbox at all. Happy Thanksgiving, I guess.

title: Everything I know about writing
content:
1.

A few years ago, some researchers put ants and humans in a head-to-head battle of wits. The task was to maneuver an awkwardly sized object through a series of obstacles, like this:

Humans and ants competed both as individuals and in groups. The humans were forbidden from communicating with one another (I guess to make the playing field more level with the ants?), and they were made to wear sunglasses and masks to prevent any nonverbal signals. The ants were allowed to do whatever they wanted, on account of them being ants. Researchers “incubated” the objects in cat food and rubbed them with tuna to make them “seem like attractive food items to the ants” (I assume humans were spared this step).

I have read the paper multiple times and I still don’t really understand why they did any of this, but the videos they made are really cool:

I bring this up because watching those videos, I think to myself: that’s exactly what writing is. It’s maneuvering an awkwardly sized idea into someone’s head. It’s getting the thing wedged in the wrong spot and then backing up to reorient it. It’s wondering why something that looks so easy can be so hard. And occasionally, the whole thing reeks of tuna.

2.

Trying to write drives most people nuts, but nobody ever told me that there’s a good nuts and a bad nuts.

Bad nuts is when you’re sitting there thinking the same thing over and over again, or thinking nothing at all, just drumming your fingers on the desk and checking your email every 17 seconds, like “hmm...words...words...what is a word...”. This is both painful and pointless.

Good nuts is when you’re trying a million things a minute and almost all of them are failing. Like:

Does it go like this?

No.

Does it go like this?

No.

Does it go like THIS?

No.

Does it go like t*h*i*s?

No.

Does it go like T~H~I~S?

YES

This is also painful, but it ultimately results in something that you want to show other people. In this way, it is very similar to getting your unibrow waxed.

title: Becoming Skilled at Making Documents
content:
The vast majority of the documents people use to do business are really quite poor. Presentations that make your eyes glaze over, memos that are inscrutable or unclear, and all kinds of artifacts that say more about how they were created than whatever message they were ostensibly trying to communicate. It's been one of my great frustrations for years, and a big part of why I wrote Make Better Documents a while ago. That post captured a list of the suggestions I've been giving people for years on how to make better, more effective documents that can actually do work for you, instead of fighting at cross purposes to your larger goals.

To my great surprise, that list of suggestions on how to make better documents got a pretty huge response, and a lot of people told me they found it really helpful. So now, I've created a Better Documents skills.md file for people who use LLM tools like Claude to help assist them in creating business documents, to prompt their AI tools to make better documents by default.

If you're not familiar, agent skills are simple text files that describe new capabilities or processes that LLMs can take advantage of when carrying out tasks. (They're Markdown files — more proof of how Markdown is taking over the world!) The way this skill works is that it's distilled the broad principles I outlined in that post into a series of 5 tests, covering areas like whether you've properly considered your target audience, whether the overall structure is correct, if you've overdone things with your formatting, and if things are named clearly, and then either generates a new file that follows those rules, or reviews an existing document to make sure it is obeying best practices.

It's nothing too fancy, but I've been using it for a while, and shared it with a few friends, and people have told me they found it handy and it's improved some of their routine documents. I'm especially glad that people have found it useful even if they're the kind of folks who would never let an LLM generate a document on their behalf, but do think software tools are useful for things like spell check or grammar check. I see this as being a tool in that kind of category.

If you're familiar with skills, the install process is really simple and works just like any other skill. This skill is totally free and open source (if you have improvements, send along a pull request on GitHub, or if you're not a coder type, just email me or hit me up on social media and let me know what fixes/suggestions you've got), so there are no encumbrances or restrictions on its use. I am curious if it's useful to people, especially if you find it handy to use more broadly at a company, so don't be shy to get in touch if you find it valuable.

Here's to us all enduring fewer terrible presentations!
